headline: Pulled Off the Deep Drops, Worked the Shelf Edge — Yellowfin and a Mahi to Show for It
subhead: Bigeye chunking went quiet overnight, so we shifted daylight hours to the shelf break and found scattered but real action.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to skip our usual overnight anchor-up in the deep water and instead spend daylight hours working the shelf break on the troll. That's not how we've fished Wilmington most of this summer, but the numbers on the overnight chunk had gotten thin enough that burning fuel to sit still didn't make sense anymore. If the bigeye aren't cooperating after dark, I'd rather run bait spreads over structure I can actually see moving on the fish finder than hope a chunk slick pulls something up from a thousand feet of water that isn't there.

That decision paid off, modestly. We picked up three yellowfin in the 25 to 40 pound class trolling green machines and cedar plugs behind a spreader bar, worked tight along a temperature seam that's been sitting just east of the canyon's edge. The water out there has a warm pool parked on it that hasn't wanted to move, and that's the same warm pool that's been giving the whole area trouble all month — it's flattened out the color and temperature breaks that usually stack bait up over the deeper humps. What it has done is push some of the activity shallower, onto the shelf itself, which is exactly where we found our fish. One mahi, a stout bull pushing 20 pounds, came off a small grass patch holding some scattered floating debris — that's been the pattern for mahi lately, small isolated debris fields rather than big weed lines, so you've got to run visual and be ready to peel off the spread when you spot something.

Bigeye have been the frustrating story. We ran the chunk for four hours one night this week — butterflied bunker, a sabiki-caught bait or two mixed in, drifting a natural slick off the stern — and came up with one fish in the 120-pound range and a couple of short bites we never connected on. That's a long way from where this bite was running a few weeks back. The thermal boundary that's been sitting east of the canyon hasn't broken down, but it hasn't organized into anything productive either — it's just sitting there, flat and unhelpful, and until it either retreats or reshuffles, I'm not optimistic about the overnight numbers improving much. If you're set up to chunk, I'd still put in the time, because one or two quality bigeye is still a good trip for most boats. Just don't go in expecting a repeat of July.

White marlin have stayed a realistic bonus fish on the troll, not a target you can plan a trip around but one you'll see if you're pulling a naked ballyhoo spread with a couple of dredge teasers mixed in along any real temperature break. We had two bites in six days out, converted one, a fish right around 60 pounds that came unglued twice before finally sticking on a small ballyhoo skirted in pink and white. No wahoo this week for us, though I heard of one boat picking up a pair on high-speed lures worked over structure closer to the shelf edge — worth keeping a wahoo bomb rigged if you're already running that speed for marlin.

The honest read here is that Wilmington is fishing like a lot of the mid-Atlantic canyons right now — spotty, not dead, but nowhere close to lit-up. The traditional deep drops that usually load up this time of year have gone quiet, and from what I'm seeing and hearing, that's a widespread problem, not just a Wilmington issue. The fish that are around have moved up onto the shelf break, which tells me the warm pool sitting offshore of the canyon is squeezing the productive water into a narrower band than we're used to working. That's actually useful information — it means less running around guessing and more time working a specific stretch of water carefully.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason to change the plan much for the next several days. If that thermal boundary holds where it's sitting, I'd keep running daylight troll spreads along the shelf edge rather than committing full nights to the chunk — better use of fuel and time on the water for what's actually biting. If it breaks down or slides, and there's some chance of that given how long it's been parked there, I'd expect the deeper lumps to come back into play and the bigeye chunk bite to pick back up with it. That's the single biggest variable I'm watching this week — where that warm water sits three days from now will tell us whether we're back on the anchor after dark or staying on the troll through the shelf break. Bring dramamine either way; the ride out has been lumpy the last few trips and doesn't look like it's smoothing out soon.
